extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media critics, and informed readers interested in journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative standards for evaluating plagiarism in news reporting, illustrated by the Sari Horwitz/Washington Post case; covers ethical rules, harms, verification responsibilities, and typical newsroom consequences and corrections practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mitigating circumstances for plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are no mitigating circumstances for plagiarism.” (Quoted from Washington Post Executive Editor Marcus Brauchli.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute, zero-tolerance stance: plagiarism is unacceptable regardless of deadline pressure, personal stress, or other excuses. The page uses Brauchli’s quote to justify swift disciplinary action (example: three-month suspension) and rejects explanations as exculpatory. Anti-pattern: accepting deadline stress or personal issues as sufficient excuse for copying another outlet’s text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism injures readers (primary victims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism’s most aggrieved victims are readers, who trust that copy filed under a byline accurately reports the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: when a reporter copies another outlet, readers may be misinformed (if the original erred), denied better reporting (if the original was mediocre), or unable to judge the reporter’s competence. Evaluate plagiarism incidents primarily by the harm done to readers’ trust and access to accurate, original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using another outlet’s work as your own is wrong and inexcusable
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting another newspaper’s work “as if it were my own” is characterized as wrong and inexcusable in the reporter’s apology and by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative rule for bylined reporting: do not present competitors’ text, explanation, or wording as your own. Even when copied passages are explanatory or ‘boilerplate,’ passing them off as original violates journalistic ethics. Example: Horwitz’s apology is cited but deemed insufficient to excuse the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealing another reporter’s understanding or interpretation is plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if wording is plain or boilerplate, appropriating another reporter’s understanding of a case (their grasp/interpretation) constitutes stealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between mere identical phrasing and theft of interpretive work: copying someone’s clear explanatory synthesis (their 'understanding') and claiming it as your own is unethical. Anti-pattern: claiming that copied material was merely 'boilerplate' to avoid culpability; the author argues that the underlying understanding was still stolen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters should verify primary documents and rely on original staff reporting rather than reprinting competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers assign staff to cover stories (rather than running wire or reprinting competitors) because they believe their staffers will produce better, more thoroughly verified reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation: reporters must inspect supporting legal documents and original sources themselves rather than lifting competitor copy. If a reporter copies without verifying, readers cannot be confident in the accuracy. Editorial practice implied: use your newsroom’s reporting resources to produce original coverage; do not substitute competitor copy under a staff byline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism defrauds the employer/newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: By stealing competitor copy and calling it her own, the reporter 'defrauded the Post' — harming the newspaper’s standing and editorial mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer-level harm: plagiarism undermines the paper’s claim that it supplies better, original reporting. Consequence for internal evaluation: plagiarism is a breach of trust with the institution and justifies disciplinary measures; though the author notes this harm is less severe than the harm to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences: disciplinary actions are warranted but industry may permit career recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism can lead to punishments (example given: a three-month suspension; possible firing), but the news industry is generally tolerant and offenders often find work again if they accept punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of incidents should include appropriate sanctions (suspension, termination in severe cases) and recognition that confession, contrition, and time often permit professional recovery. The column cites the Post’s swift suspension as an example and references historical tolerance (Columbia Journalism Review piece).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, editor’s notes, and transparent tracking of errors are required responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should publish notes explaining plagiarism incidents and provide mechanisms to notify readers of corrections (example: the Post’s editor’s note; Slate’s RSS feed and email instructions for tracking corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial practices: issue an editor’s note explaining the finding; correct the record; offer readers ways to track corrections (RSS, email alerts). Transparency about errors and corrections is part of ethical newsroom response and helps restore reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism reduces reporting quality and deprives readers of better work
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reporter copies mediocre or erroneous competitor copy, readers suffer because they miss the chance to read higher-quality reporting or are exposed to mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the impact of plagiarism, consider whether the copied material was inferior or inaccurate relative to what original reporting would have produced. This is an evaluative criterion for judging the severity of harm to readers and the public record.
